chunks.text: Butea monosperma belongs to the pea family, Fabaceae (subfamily Faboideae). It is native to tropical and subtropical South and Southeast Asia, found across Bangladesh, India, Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, Malaysia and western Indonesia. It is a modest, slow-growing deciduous tree reaching about 15 metres, with pinnate leaves made of three large leaflets 10–20 cm each. Its defining feature is a mass of bright orange-red, 2.5 cm flowers borne in racemes up to 15 cm long on otherwise bare branches, typically blooming between February and April — though a given tree does not flower every year. Flat, 15–20 cm pods follow the flowers.

The flowers yield butein, a vivid orange-red dye long used to colour silk and sometimes cotton, and are the traditional source of the 'kesari' colour thrown during Holi celebrations. The tree's gum, known as kamarkas, is used in food preparation, and a traditional drink called Palash sharbat, made from the flowers, is described in Ayurvedic tradition as helping the body cope with heat. The soft, spongy, dirty-white timber is not commercially valuable as general lumber but is notably durable underwater, so it has traditionally been used for well curbs and water scoops.

Ecologically, the tree is an important host for the lac insect (Laccifer lacca), which secretes the resin used to make shellac, and Palash-grown lac is noted for high yield per hectare. It is considered sacred in both Hinduism and Buddhism and is the state flower of Jharkhand. Historically, dense 'dhak' forests of this tree covered the Doaba region of north India before being cleared for agriculture in the 19th century. The tree also appears in classical Sanskrit literature, including the Rigveda and Yajurveda, and features in the Bengali poetry of Rabindranath Tagore.
